description: Economics question bank for Karnataka FDA & SDA Examinations based on Chapter 4.3 notes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is economics?

options.A: A natural science that studies the physical world
options.B: A social science that studies how individuals, firms, governments and societies make choices about allocating scarce resources
options.C: The study of money and banking only
options.D: The study of political systems and governance

questions.explanation: Economics is a social science that studies how individuals, firms, governments and societies make choices about the allocation of scarce resources among competing uses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the central economic problem?

options.A: Inflation
options.B: Unemployment
options.C: Scarcity
options.D: Poverty

questions.explanation: The central economic problem is scarcity: resources are limited while human wants are numerous, so choices and trade-offs are unavoidable.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are the three basic economic questions?

options.A: When to produce, where to produce, and how much to produce
options.B: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
options.C: Why to produce, who to produce for, and when to produce
options.D: How much to produce, what to consume, and who to trade with

questions.explanation: The three basic economic questions are: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is opportunity cost?

options.A: The total cost of producing a good
options.B: The value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made
options.C: The cost of goods that are available for free
options.D: The price of a good in the market

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is marginal analysis?

options.A: Analysis of the total benefit of an activity
options.B: Comparison of the additional benefit and additional cost arising from one more unit of an activity
options.C: Analysis of the average cost of production
options.D: Study of the market as a whole

questions.explanation: Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost arising from one more unit of an activity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What does ceteris paribus mean?

options.A: Everything changes simultaneously
options.B: Other things remaining equal
options.C: All men are created equal
options.D: The market is always right

questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus means other things remaining equal; economists use it to isolate the relationship between selected variables.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a positive economic statement?

options.A: A statement about what ought to be
options.B: A descriptive and testable statement about what is or what happens
options.C: A statement that is always true
options.D: A statement based on value judgments

questions.explanation: A positive economic statement is descriptive and testable in principle; it concerns what is or what happens.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a normative economic statement?

options.A: A statement that can be tested with data
options.B: A statement about what is
options.C: A statement expressing a value judgment about what ought to be
options.D: A statement about the normal state of the economy

questions.explanation: A normative economic statement expresses a value judgment about what ought to be.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is microeconomics?

options.A: Study of economy-wide variables such as national income
options.B: Study of individual consumers, firms, particular markets and allocation of resources at the unit or market level
options.C: Study of international trade only
options.D: Study of government budgets

questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies individual consumers, firms, particular markets and the allocation of resources at the unit or market level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is macroeconomics?

options.A: Study of individual consumer behaviour
options.B: Study of single firms and markets
options.C: Study of economy-wide variables such as national income, aggregate output, inflation, unemployment and economic growth
options.D: Study of household budgeting

questions.explanation: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide variables such as national income, aggregate output, inflation, unemployment and economic growth.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Who is widely known as the father of modern economics?

options.A: John Maynard Keynes
options.B: Alfred Marshall
options.C: Adam Smith
options.D: David Ricardo

questions.explanation: Adam Smith is widely known as the father of modern economics, particularly for his work 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' (1776).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Who wrote 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money'?

options.A: Adam Smith
options.B: John Maynard Keynes
options.C: Alfred Marshall
options.D: Thomas Robert Malthus

questions.explanation: John Maynard Keynes wrote 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', published in 1936.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Who wrote 'Principles of Economics' (1890)?

options.A: Adam Smith
options.B: David Ricardo
options.C: Alfred Marshall
options.D: John Maynard Keynes

questions.explanation: Alfred Marshall wrote 'Principles of Economics' in 1890.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Who is associated with the concept of the invisible hand?

options.A: John Maynard Keynes
options.B: Adam Smith
options.C: Karl Marx
options.D: Alfred Marshall

questions.explanation: Adam Smith used the expression 'invisible hand' in explaining how individual actions can sometimes produce wider economic effects.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an economic good?

options.A: A good that is available in unlimited quantity
options.B: A good or service that is scarce relative to demand and therefore has an opportunity cost
options.C: A good produced only by the government
options.D: A good that has no price

questions.explanation: An economic good is a good or service that is scarce relative to demand and therefore has an opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a free good in elementary economics?

options.A: A good provided free of cost by the government
options.B: A good available in sufficient abundance at a particular time and place that no sacrifice is required to obtain it
options.C: A good that is not scarce anywhere in the world
options.D: A good that has zero utility

questions.explanation: A free good is available in sufficient abundance at a particular time and place that no sacrifice is required to obtain it; this is a context-dependent concept.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a capital good?

options.A: A good purchased for final consumption by households
options.B: A produced asset used to produce other goods or services, such as machinery, tools and factory buildings
options.C: A good that is consumed quickly
options.D: A good that is free of cost

questions.explanation: A capital good is a produced asset used to produce other goods or services, such as machinery, tools and factory buildings.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a consumer good?

options.A: A good used to produce other goods
options.B: A good purchased for final use by households rather than for further production
options.C: A good used as an input in production
options.D: A good that lasts for a very long time

questions.explanation: A consumer good is a good purchased for final use by households rather than for further production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an intermediate good?

options.A: A good purchased for final consumption
options.B: A good that lasts for an extended period
options.C: An input used up or transformed in the production of another good or service during the accounting period
options.D: A good that is exported to other countries

questions.explanation: An intermediate good is an input used up or transformed in the production of another good or service during the accounting period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a durable good?

options.A: A good that is consumed quickly
options.B: A good that provides services over an extended period, such as a refrigerator or vehicle
options.C: A good used only in production
options.D: A good that cannot be stored

questions.explanation: A durable good is a good that provides services over an extended period, such as a refrigerator or vehicle.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a non-durable good?

options.A: A good that lasts for many years
options.B: A good generally consumed or used up quickly, such as food or fuel
options.C: A good used to produce other goods
options.D: A good that is not scarce

questions.explanation: A non-durable good is a good generally consumed or used up quickly, such as food or fuel.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an economic system?

options.A: The set of institutions and arrangements through which production, distribution and consumption are organised
options.B: The study of money and banking
options.C: The system of government in a country
options.D: The set of laws governing trade

questions.explanation: An economic system is the set of institutions and arrangements through which production, distribution and consumption are organised.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a capitalist economy?

options.A: An economy that relies substantially on private ownership, markets, profit incentives and decentralised economic decisions
options.B: An economy that gives a substantial role to social or public ownership and collective planning
options.C: An economy that combines private enterprise and markets with public ownership and regulation
options.D: An economy that is completely controlled by the government

questions.explanation: A capitalist economy relies substantially on private ownership, markets, profit incentives and decentralised economic decisions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a socialist economy?

options.A: An economy that relies substantially on private ownership and markets
options.B: An economy that gives a substantial role to social or public ownership and collective planning in organising production and distribution
options.C: An economy that combines private enterprise and markets with public ownership
options.D: An economy with no government intervention

questions.explanation: A socialist economy gives a substantial role to social or public ownership and collective planning in organising production and distribution.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a mixed economy?

options.A: An economy that relies only on private enterprise and markets
options.B: An economy that relies only on public ownership and central planning
options.C: An economy that combines private enterprise and markets with public ownership, regulation, taxation and government provision of services
options.D: An economy that has no government

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private enterprise and markets with public ownership, regulation, taxation and government provision of services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are the four factors of production?

options.A: Money, land, labour and capital
options.B: Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship
options.C: Land, labour, money and technology
options.D: Capital, entrepreneurship, money and government

questions.explanation: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship or organisation.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is land as a factor of production?

options.A: Only the soil used for farming
options.B: Natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, forests, minerals and other gifts of nature
options.C: Buildings and factories
options.D: Money used for investment

questions.explanation: Land includes natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, forests, minerals and other gifts of nature.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is labour as a factor of production?

options.A: Machinery used in production
options.B: The physical and mental human effort used to produce goods and services
options.C: Natural resources used in production
options.D: The risk-taking ability of entrepreneurs

questions.explanation: Labour is the physical and mental human effort used to produce goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is capital as a factor of production?

options.A: Natural resources used in production
options.B: Human effort used in production
options.C: Produced assets used to produce other goods and services, such as machinery, buildings and tools
options.D: Money used for consumption

questions.explanation: Capital consists of produced assets used to produce other goods and services, such as machinery, buildings and tools.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is entrepreneurship?

options.A: The activity of organising other factors of production, making business decisions, innovating and bearing business risks
options.B: The physical effort of workers
options.C: The use of natural resources in production
options.D: The accumulation of capital goods

questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship is the activity of organising other factors of production, making business decisions, innovating and bearing business risks.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are factor incomes?

options.A: Payments to factors of production: wages to labour, rent to land, interest to capital and profit to entrepreneurship
options.B: Income earned only by workers
options.C: Income earned from exports
options.D: Government revenue from taxes

questions.explanation: Factor incomes are payments to factors of production: wages to labour, rent to land, interest to capital in the traditional classification, and profit to entrepreneurship.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is utility?

options.A: The satisfaction or want-satisfying capacity that a consumer derives from consuming a good or service
options.B: The usefulness of a good in production
options.C: The price of a good
options.D: The cost of producing a good

questions.explanation: Utility is the satisfaction or want-satisfying capacity that a consumer derives from consuming a good or service.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is total utility?

options.A: The satisfaction from consuming one additional unit
options.B: The overall satisfaction obtained from consuming a given quantity of a good or service
options.C: The total cost of producing a good
options.D: The total revenue from selling a good

questions.explanation: Total utility is the overall satisfaction obtained from consuming a given quantity of a good or service.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is marginal utility?

options.A: The overall satisfaction from consuming a good
options.B: The additional utility obtained from consuming one additional unit of a good or service
options.C: The total utility divided by the quantity consumed
options.D: The utility derived from free goods

questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the additional utility obtained from consuming one additional unit of a good or service.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the law of diminishing marginal utility?

options.A: As a person consumes more of a good, total utility always increases
options.B: Other things remaining equal, as a person consumes successive units of a good during a given period, the additional satisfaction from each additional unit tends to decline
options.C: Marginal utility is always constant
options.D: Marginal utility is always negative

questions.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, other things remaining equal, as a person consumes successive units of a good during a given period, the additional satisfaction from each additional unit tends to decline.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the law of equi-marginal utility?

options.A: A consumer maximises utility when total utility is maximised
options.B: A consumer maximises utility under a budget constraint when the marginal utility per unit of money spent is equalised across goods
options.C: A consumer maximises utility when marginal utility is zero
options.D: A consumer maximises utility by consuming only one good

questions.explanation: A consumer maximises utility under a budget constraint when the marginal utility per unit of money spent is equalised across goods, subject to the assumptions of the model.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a production possibility frontier (PPF)?

options.A: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with given resources and technology when resources are used efficiently
options.B: A curve showing the minimum cost of production
options.C: A curve showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded
options.D: A curve showing the relationship between income and consumption

questions.explanation: A PPF shows the maximum combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with given resources and technology when resources are used efficiently.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What does a point inside the PPF indicate?

options.A: Productive efficiency
options.B: Underutilisation or inefficient use of available resources
options.C: An unattainable combination of goods
options.D: Economic growth

questions.explanation: A point inside the PPF indicates underutilisation or inefficient use of available resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What does a point on the PPF indicate?

options.A: Inefficiency
options.B: Unattainability
options.C: Productive efficiency given the available resources and technology
options.D: Unemployment

questions.explanation: A point on the PPF indicates productive efficiency given the available resources and technology.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What does a point outside the PPF indicate?

options.A: Productive efficiency
options.B: Underutilisation of resources
options.C: An unattainable combination with existing resources and technology
options.D: Economic recession

questions.explanation: A point outside the current PPF is unattainable with existing resources and technology.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What causes the PPF to shift outward?

options.A: An increase in resources, improvements in technology, better skills or productivity growth
options.B: A decrease in resources
options.C: An increase in unemployment
options.D: A decrease in technology

questions.explanation: An increase in resources, improvements in technology, better skills or productivity growth can shift the PPF outward.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is economic efficiency?

options.A: Using resources so that output or welfare is maximised relative to available resources and technology
options.B: Maximising the cost of production
options.C: Producing only consumer goods
options.D: Producing only capital goods

questions.explanation: Economic efficiency concerns using resources so that output or welfare is maximised relative to available resources and technology.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is allocative efficiency?

options.A: Producing at the lowest possible cost
options.B: A situation where the composition of output reflects consumer preferences and marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost
options.C: Producing maximum output with given resources
options.D: Achieving full employment

questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency occurs when the composition of output reflects consumer preferences and the marginal social benefit of production equals its marginal social cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is productivity?

options.A: The total output produced
options.B: The amount of output produced per unit of input, such as output per worker or output per hour
options.C: The total cost of production
options.D: The profit earned by a firm

questions.explanation: Productivity is the amount of output produced per unit of input, such as output per worker or output per hour.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is specialisation?

options.A: Concentrating production or work on a narrower set of tasks or products to improve skill, efficiency or output
options.B: Producing all goods and services within a single firm
options.C: Diversifying production across many unrelated products
options.D: Importing all goods from other countries

questions.explanation: Specialisation is concentrating production or work on a narrower set of tasks or products to improve skill, efficiency or output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a trade-off?

options.A: A situation where gaining more of one objective or good requires sacrificing some of another
options.B: A situation where all wants can be satisfied
options.C: A situation where there is no scarcity
options.D: A situation where prices are constant

questions.explanation: A trade-off occurs when gaining more of one objective or good requires sacrificing some of another.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is production?

options.A: The process of combining inputs to create goods and services or to add value and utility
options.B: The process of consuming goods and services
options.C: The process of distributing income
options.D: The process of exchanging goods in a market

questions.explanation: Production is the process of combining inputs to create goods and services or to add value and utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a production function?

options.A: A function that expresses the maximum output obtainable from given quantities of inputs, with technology held constant
options.B: A function that shows the relationship between price and quantity supplied
options.C: A function that shows the relationship between income and consumption
options.D: A function that shows the cost of production

questions.explanation: A production function expresses the maximum output obtainable from given quantities of inputs, with technology held constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the short run in production theory?

options.A: A period in which all factors of production can be varied
options.B: A period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
options.C: A period of less than one year
options.D: A period in which technology changes

questions.explanation: The short run is a period in which at least one factor of production is fixed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the long run in production theory?

options.A: A period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
options.B: A period of more than ten years
options.C: A period in which all factors of production can be varied
options.D: A period in which output is constant

questions.explanation: The long run is a period in which all factors of production can be varied.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is fixed cost?

options.A: Cost that changes with the level of output
options.B: Cost that does not vary with the level of output over the relevant short-run range, such as rent on a factory under a fixed contract
options.C: The total cost of production
options.D: The additional cost of producing one more unit

questions.explanation: Fixed cost does not vary with the level of output over the relevant short-run range, such as rent on a factory under a fixed contract.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is variable cost?

options.A: Cost that does not change with output
options.B: Cost that changes with the level of output, such as raw materials or piece-rate labour
options.C: The total cost of production
options.D: The average cost of production

questions.explanation: Variable cost changes with the level of output, such as raw materials or piece-rate labour.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is total cost?

options.A: The sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost
options.B: The cost of producing one additional unit
options.C: The cost per unit of output
options.D: The cost of fixed factors only

questions.explanation: Total cost is the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is average cost?

options.A: Total cost divided by the quantity of output
options.B: The additional cost of producing one more unit
options.C: The sum of fixed and variable costs
options.D: The cost of fixed factors only

questions.explanation: Average cost is total cost divided by the quantity of output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is marginal cost?

options.A: The total cost of production
options.B: The additional cost of producing one more unit of output
options.C: The average cost of production
options.D: The fixed cost of production

questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the additional cost of producing one more unit of output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is total product?

options.A: The total quantity of output produced by a given set of inputs
options.B: The output produced by one additional unit of input
options.C: The output per unit of input
options.D: The total cost of production

questions.explanation: Total product is the total quantity of output produced by a given set of inputs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is average product of labour?

options.A: Total output divided by the quantity of labour employed
options.B: The additional output produced by employing one additional unit of labour
options.C: The total cost divided by the quantity of labour
options.D: The total output multiplied by the quantity of labour

questions.explanation: Average product of labour is total output divided by the quantity of labour employed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is marginal product of labour?

options.A: Total output divided by the quantity of labour
options.B: The additional output produced by employing one additional unit of labour, holding other inputs constant
options.C: The total cost of labour
options.D: The average output per worker

questions.explanation: Marginal product of labour is the additional output produced by employing one additional unit of labour, holding other inputs constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the law of variable proportions?

options.A: In the short run, when one factor is varied while other factors remain fixed, marginal product may initially rise and eventually decline as more of the variable factor is employed
options.B: In the long run, all factors are varied in the same proportion
options.C: Output always increases proportionately with inputs
options.D: Marginal product is always constant

questions.explanation: The law of variable proportions states that in the short run, when one factor is varied while other factors remain fixed, marginal product may initially rise and eventually decline as more of the variable factor is employed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are returns to scale?

options.A: How output changes when all inputs are increased in the same proportion in the long run
options.B: How output changes when one input is increased while others are fixed
options.C: The relationship between cost and output
options.D: The relationship between price and quantity supplied

questions.explanation: Returns to scale describe how output changes when all inputs are increased in the same proportion in the long run.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are increasing returns to scale?

options.A: When a given percentage increase in all inputs produces a larger percentage increase in output
options.B: When output increases in the same proportion as all inputs
options.C: When output increases by a smaller percentage than the proportional increase in all inputs
options.D: When output decreases as inputs increase

questions.explanation: Increasing returns to scale occur when a given percentage increase in all inputs produces a larger percentage increase in output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are constant returns to scale?

options.A: When output increases by a larger percentage than inputs
options.B: When output increases in the same proportion as all inputs
options.C: When output increases by a smaller percentage than inputs
options.D: When output remains constant regardless of inputs

questions.explanation: Constant returns to scale occur when output increases in the same proportion as all inputs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are decreasing returns to scale?

options.A: When output increases by a larger percentage than inputs
options.B: When output increases in the same proportion as inputs
options.C: When output increases by a smaller percentage than the proportional increase in all inputs
options.D: When output remains constant

questions.explanation: Decreasing returns to scale occur when output increases by a smaller percentage than the proportional increase in all inputs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is division of labour in production?

options.A: The allocation of different stages or tasks in production to specialised workers or units
options.B: The division of profits among workers
options.C: The division of output among consumers
options.D: The division of a firm into departments

questions.explanation: Division of labour in production is the allocation of different stages or tasks in production to specialised workers or units.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is industrial production?

options.A: The cultivation of crops and rearing of livestock
options.B: The creation or processing of goods through manufacturing, mining, utilities or related industrial activities
options.C: The provision of services such as banking and education
options.D: The extraction of minerals only

questions.explanation: Industrial production is the creation or processing of goods through manufacturing, mining, utilities or related industrial activities.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is agricultural production?

options.A: The creation of goods through manufacturing
options.B: The cultivation of crops and the rearing of livestock and related farm output
options.C: The provision of banking services
options.D: The extraction of minerals

questions.explanation: Agricultural production is the cultivation of crops and the rearing of livestock and related farm output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is value added?

options.A: The value of output minus the value of intermediate consumption used to produce it
options.B: The total value of output
options.C: The value of intermediate goods only
options.D: The value of fixed capital

questions.explanation: Value added is the value of output minus the value of intermediate consumption used to produce it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Why is value added important in national income accounting?

options.A: Summing value added across production units avoids double counting intermediate goods
options.B: It measures the total value of intermediate goods
options.C: It measures the total value of final goods only
options.D: It measures the value of imports

questions.explanation: Summing value added across production units avoids double counting intermediate goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are economies of scale?

options.A: Increases in average cost that may occur when an organisation becomes too large
options.B: Reductions in average cost that can occur as the scale of production increases
options.C: Increases in total cost as output increases
options.D: Constant average cost at all levels of output

questions.explanation: Economies of scale are reductions in average cost that can occur as the scale of production increases.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are diseconomies of scale?

options.A: Reductions in average cost as production increases
options.B: Increases in average cost that may occur when an organisation becomes too large or complex to manage efficiently
options.C: Constant average cost at all levels of output
options.D: Decreases in total cost as output increases

questions.explanation: Diseconomies of scale are increases in average cost that may occur when an organisation becomes too large or complex to manage efficiently.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is consumption?

options.A: The use of goods and services by households or other final users to satisfy wants
options.B: The production of goods and services
options.C: The distribution of income
options.D: The exchange of goods in a market

questions.explanation: Consumption is the use of goods and services by households or other final users to satisfy wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a consumer?

options.A: A person or household that purchases or uses goods and services
options.B: A firm that produces goods
options.C: A government agency that regulates markets
options.D: A worker who produces goods

questions.explanation: A consumer is a person or household that purchases or uses goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a consumption function in macroeconomics?

options.A: A function that describes the relationship between aggregate consumption expenditure and variables such as disposable income
options.B: A function that describes the relationship between price and quantity demanded
options.C: A function that describes the relationship between output and inputs
options.D: A function that describes the relationship between tax rates and revenue

questions.explanation: A consumption function describes the relationship between aggregate consumption expenditure and variables such as disposable income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is disposable income?

options.A: Personal income remaining after direct personal taxes
options.B: Total income before taxes
options.C: Income from investments only
options.D: Income earned by the government

questions.explanation: Disposable income is personal income remaining after direct personal taxes, with the exact statistical definition depending on the national accounts framework.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is autonomous consumption?

options.A: The part of consumption that changes with disposable income
options.B: The part of consumption that does not vary with current disposable income in a simple Keynesian consumption model
options.C: The total consumption expenditure
options.D: The consumption of durable goods only

questions.explanation: Autonomous consumption is the part of consumption that does not vary with current disposable income in a simple Keynesian consumption model.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is induced consumption?

options.A: The part of consumption that does not vary with income
options.B: The part of consumption that changes with disposable income
options.C: The total consumption expenditure
options.D: The consumption of non-durable goods only

questions.explanation: Induced consumption is the part of consumption that changes with disposable income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC)?

options.A: Consumption divided by disposable income
options.B: The change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income
options.C: The change in saving divided by the change in disposable income
options.D: Saving divided by disposable income

questions.explanation: MPC is the change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income: MPC = ΔC / ΔYd.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the average propensity to consume (APC)?

options.A: Consumption divided by disposable income
options.B: The change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income
options.C: Saving divided by disposable income
options.D: The change in saving divided by the change in disposable income

questions.explanation: APC is consumption divided by disposable income: APC = C / Yd.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is saving?

options.A: The part of disposable income not spent on current consumption
options.B: The total income earned
options.C: The total consumption expenditure
options.D: The taxes paid to the government

questions.explanation: Saving is the part of disposable income not spent on current consumption.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the marginal propensity to save (MPS)?

options.A: Saving divided by disposable income
options.B: The change in saving divided by the change in disposable income
options.C: The change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income
options.D: Consumption divided by disposable income

questions.explanation: MPS is the change in saving divided by the change in disposable income: MPS = ΔS / ΔYd.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: In the simple model where income is either consumed or saved, what is the relationship between MPC and MPS?

options.A: MPC + MPS = 1
options.B: MPC - MPS = 1
options.C: MPC × MPS = 1
options.D: MPC + MPS = 0

questions.explanation: In the simple model where income is either consumed or saved, MPC + MPS = 1.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the average propensity to save (APS)?

options.A: Saving divided by disposable income
options.B: The change in saving divided by the change in disposable income
options.C: Consumption divided by disposable income
options.D: The change in consumption divided by the change in disposable income

questions.explanation: APS is saving divided by disposable income: APS = S / Yd.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the paradox of thrift?

options.A: If everyone tries to save more at the same time during a downturn, aggregate demand and income may fall, so total realised saving may not increase
options.B: Saving always leads to economic growth
options.C: Thrift always increases national income
options.D: Saving is always equal to investment

questions.explanation: The paradox of thrift is the possibility that if everyone tries to save more at the same time during a downturn, aggregate demand and income may fall, so total realised saving may not increase.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is consumer behaviour?

options.A: The study of how individuals and households choose, purchase and use goods and services
options.B: The study of how firms produce goods
options.C: The study of government taxation
options.D: The study of international trade

questions.explanation: Consumer behaviour studies how individuals and households choose, purchase and use goods and services.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a budget constraint?

options.A: A constraint that represents the combinations of goods a consumer can afford with a given income and given prices
options.B: A limit on government spending
options.C: A limit on production
options.D: A limit on imports

questions.explanation: A budget constraint represents the combinations of goods a consumer can afford with a given income and given prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is consumer surplus?

options.A: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
options.B: The total amount consumers pay for a good
options.C: The total utility derived from a good
options.D: The cost of producing a good

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a substitute good?

options.A: A good that is consumed together with another good
options.B: A good that can be used in place of another good; an increase in the price of one may raise demand for the other
options.C: A good that is always cheaper than other goods
options.D: A good that has no close substitutes

questions.explanation: A substitute good can be used in place of another good; an increase in the price of one may raise demand for the other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a complementary good?

options.A: A good that can be used in place of another good
options.B: A good that is consumed together with another good; an increase in the price of one may reduce demand for the other
options.C: A good that is always consumed alone
options.D: A good that has many substitutes

questions.explanation: A complementary good is consumed together with another good; an increase in the price of one may reduce demand for the other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is conspicuous consumption?

options.A: Spending intended partly to display wealth or social status, a concept associated with Thorstein Veblen
options.B: Consumption of basic necessities
options.C: Consumption of government-provided goods
options.D: Consumption of imported goods only

questions.explanation: Conspicuous consumption is spending intended partly to display wealth or social status, a concept associated with Thorstein Veblen.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is distribution in economics?

options.A: The process through which income and output are allocated among individuals, households and factors of production
options.B: The process of producing goods and services
options.C: The process of consuming goods and services
options.D: The process of exchanging goods in a market

questions.explanation: Distribution is the process through which income and output are allocated among individuals, households and factors of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is functional distribution of income?

options.A: How income is distributed among individuals regardless of the source
options.B: How national income is divided among factors of production, such as labour and capital
options.C: How income is taxed by the government
options.D: How income is spent on consumption

questions.explanation: Functional distribution explains how national income is divided among factors of production, such as labour and capital.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What are wages?

options.A: Payments received by labour for work performed
options.B: Payments received for the use of land
options.C: Payments for borrowing money
options.D: Residual return to an enterprise

questions.explanation: Wages are payments received by labour for work performed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is nominal wage?

options.A: The purchasing power of a wage
options.B: The money amount paid to a worker
options.C: The wage after accounting for inflation
options.D: The minimum wage fixed by the government

questions.explanation: Nominal wage is the money amount paid to a worker.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is real wage?

options.A: The money amount paid to a worker
options.B: The wage measured in terms of purchasing power after accounting for the price level
options.C: The wage paid in kind
options.D: The wage before taxes

questions.explanation: Real wage measures the purchasing power of a nominal wage after accounting for the price level.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is rent in classical economics?

options.A: The return attributed to the use of land or other scarce natural resources
options.B: The payment for borrowing money
options.C: The payment received by labour
options.D: The residual return to an enterprise

questions.explanation: Rent is the return attributed to the use of land or other scarce natural resources; modern usage can also refer to payments for property use.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is interest?

options.A: The payment for borrowing money or the return earned on lending or certain financial assets
options.B: The payment for the use of land
options.C: The payment received by labour
options.D: The residual return to an enterprise

questions.explanation: Interest is the payment for borrowing money or the return earned on lending or certain financial assets.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is profit?

options.A: The payment for the use of land
options.B: The residual return to an enterprise after relevant costs have been deducted from revenue
options.C: The payment for borrowing money
options.D: The payment received by labour

questions.explanation: Profit is the residual return to an enterprise after relevant costs have been deducted from revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is economic rent?

options.A: A payment to a factor of production above the minimum amount required to keep it in its current use
options.B: The rent paid for residential accommodation
options.C: The interest paid on a loan
options.D: The wage paid to a worker

questions.explanation: Economic rent is a payment to a factor of production above the minimum amount required to keep it in its current use.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is income inequality?

options.A: The uneven distribution of income among people or households
options.B: The equal distribution of income among all people
options.C: The total income of a country
options.D: The average income of a country

questions.explanation: Income inequality refers to the uneven distribution of income among people or households.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the Lorenz curve?

options.A: A graphical representation of the cumulative distribution of income or wealth across a population
options.B: A curve showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded
options.C: A curve showing the relationship between output and inputs
options.D: A curve showing the relationship between tax rates and revenue

questions.explanation: The Lorenz curve is a graphical representation of the cumulative distribution of income or wealth across a population.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the difference between income and wealth?

options.A: Income is a stock of assets; wealth is a flow received over a period
options.B: Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, net of liabilities
options.C: Income and wealth are the same thing
options.D: Income is always greater than wealth

questions.explanation: Income is a flow received over a period; wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time, net of liabilities.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is redistribution of income?

options.A: The alteration of the initial distribution of income through taxes, transfers, public services and other government policies
options.B: The distribution of income among factors of production
options.C: The distribution of income among individuals regardless of source
options.D: The measurement of income inequality

questions.explanation: Redistribution is the alteration of the initial distribution of income through taxes, transfers, public services and other government policies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a market in economics?

options.A: A physical place where goods are sold
options.B: An arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods, services or resources
options.C: A government office that regulates prices
options.D: A place where only wholesale trade occurs

questions.explanation: A market is an arrangement through which buyers and sellers interact to exchange goods, services or resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Does a market require a physical place?

options.A: Yes, a market must have a physical location
options.B: No, a market may operate physically or digitally through networks, platforms and other arrangements
options.C: Yes, only physical markets are recognized in economics
options.D: No, markets exist only in theory

questions.explanation: No. A market may operate physically or digitally through networks, platforms and other arrangements.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a perfect competition market?

options.A: A market with a single seller
options.B: A market with a few dominant firms
options.C: An ideal market structure with many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, and good information
options.D: A market with differentiated products and many sellers

questions.explanation: Perfect competition is an ideal market structure with many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, and good information.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a monopoly?

options.A: A market structure in which a single seller supplies a product with no close substitutes and significant barriers prevent entry
options.B: A market with many sellers
options.C: A market with a few sellers
options.D: A market with free entry and exit

questions.explanation: A monopoly is a market structure in which a single seller supplies a product with no close substitutes and significant barriers prevent entry.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is monopolistic competition?

options.A: A market with a single seller
options.B: A market with many sellers offering differentiated products and relatively free entry and exit
options.C: A market with a few dominant firms
options.D: A market with homogeneous products only

questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition is a market structure with many sellers offering differentiated products and relatively free entry and exit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an oligopoly?

options.A: A market with a single seller
options.B: A market with many sellers of homogeneous products
options.C: A market structure dominated by a small number of interdependent firms
options.D: A market with free entry and exit

questions.explanation: An oligopoly is a market structure dominated by a small number of interdependent firms.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a price taker?

options.A: A buyer or seller that accepts the market-determined price because it cannot individually influence it
options.B: A firm that sets its own price
options.C: A government agency that fixes prices
options.D: A consumer who refuses to pay the market price

questions.explanation: A price taker is a buyer or seller that accepts the market-determined price because it cannot individually influence it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a price maker?

options.A: A buyer or seller that accepts the market price
options.B: A firm or seller with sufficient market power to influence the price it charges
options.C: A government agency that fixes prices
options.D: A consumer who determines market demand

questions.explanation: A price maker is a firm or seller with sufficient market power to influence the price it charges.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is market equilibrium?

options.A: The price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.B: The price at which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
options.C: The price at which quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
options.D: The maximum price a consumer is willing to pay

questions.explanation: Market equilibrium is the price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is excess demand?

options.A: A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a given price
options.B: A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price
options.C: A situation where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.D: A situation where the market is in equilibrium

questions.explanation: Excess demand occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is excess supply?

options.A: A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
options.B: A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a given price
options.C: A situation where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.D: A situation where the market is in equilibrium

questions.explanation: Excess supply occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a price ceiling?

options.A: A legal minimum price; if set above the equilibrium price and enforced, it can create excess supply
options.B: A legal maximum price; if set below the equilibrium price and enforced, it can create excess demand
options.C: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.D: The price fixed by the market forces

questions.explanation: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price; if set below the equilibrium price and enforced, it can create excess demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a price floor?

options.A: A legal maximum price; if set below the equilibrium price, it can create excess demand
options.B: A legal minimum price; if set above the equilibrium price and enforced, it can create excess supply
options.C: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.D: The price determined by market forces

questions.explanation: A price floor is a legal minimum price; if set above the equilibrium price and enforced, it can create excess supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a Minimum Support Price (MSP) in India?

options.A: A government-announced price for specified crops intended to provide a price-support reference to farmers; procurement arrangements and actual access vary by crop and location
options.B: A legal maximum price for agricultural goods
options.C: The price at which agricultural goods are sold in international markets
options.D: A subsidy provided to farmers for purchasing seeds

questions.explanation: MSP is a government-announced price for specified crops intended to provide a price-support reference to farmers; procurement arrangements and actual access vary by crop and location.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a regulated market?

options.A: A market that operates under rules governing transactions, standards, licensing or market practices
options.B: A market with no government intervention
options.C: A market where prices are determined solely by supply and demand
options.D: A market that operates only in rural areas

questions.explanation: A regulated market operates under rules governing transactions, standards, licensing or market practices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a wholesale market?

options.A: A market involving sales of goods in large quantities, commonly to retailers, businesses or other intermediaries
options.B: A market involving sales of goods directly to final consumers
options.C: A market where only agricultural goods are sold
options.D: A market where only imported goods are sold

questions.explanation: A wholesale market involves sales of goods in large quantities, commonly to retailers, businesses or other intermediaries.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a retail market?

options.A: A market involving sales of goods in large quantities to businesses
options.B: A market involving sales of goods or services to final consumers
options.C: A market where only agricultural goods are sold
options.D: A market where only imported goods are sold

questions.explanation: A retail market involves sales of goods or services to final consumers.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is market failure?

options.A: A situation where unregulated market outcomes do not achieve an efficient allocation of resources, often because of externalities, public goods, market power or information problems
options.B: A situation where the market is in equilibrium
options.C: A situation where demand equals supply
options.D: A situation where prices are falling

questions.explanation: Market failure occurs when unregulated market outcomes do not achieve an efficient allocation of resources, often because of externalities, public goods, market power or information problems.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an externality?

options.A: A cost or benefit of an economic activity that affects third parties and is not fully reflected in the market price
options.B: A tax imposed on imported goods
options.C: A subsidy provided by the government
options.D: A price control imposed by the government

questions.explanation: An externality is a cost or benefit of an economic activity that affects third parties and is not fully reflected in the market price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a public good?

options.A: A good that is rival and excludable
options.B: A pure public good is non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use does not reduce another's use, and people cannot easily be excluded from benefiting
options.C: A good produced only by the government
options.D: A good that is free of cost

questions.explanation: A pure public good is non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use does not reduce another's use, and people cannot easily be excluded from benefiting.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is information asymmetry?

options.A: A situation where both parties to a transaction have equal information
options.B: A situation where one party to a transaction has more or better information than another
options.C: A situation where there is no information available
options.D: A situation where information is freely available to all

questions.explanation: Information asymmetry occurs when one party to a transaction has more or better information than another.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is demand?

options.A: The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at different prices during a given period
options.B: The total quantity of a good produced
options.C: The quantity of a good that producers are willing to sell
options.D: The price of a good in the market

questions.explanation: Demand is the quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to purchase at different prices during a given period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the law of demand?

options.A: Other things remaining equal, quantity demanded generally rises when price rises and falls when price falls
options.B: Other things remaining equal, quantity demanded generally rises when price falls and falls when price rises
options.C: Quantity demanded is always equal to quantity supplied
options.D: Quantity demanded is independent of price

questions.explanation: The law of demand states that, other things remaining equal, quantity demanded generally rises when price falls and falls when price rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Why does the demand curve generally slope downward?

options.A: Because of the substitution effect, income effect and diminishing marginal utility
options.B: Because of increasing returns to scale
options.C: Because of government regulation
options.D: Because of inflation

questions.explanation: The substitution effect, income effect and diminishing marginal utility help explain the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a demand schedule?

options.A: A table showing quantities demanded at different prices during a specified period
options.B: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded
options.C: A table showing quantities supplied at different prices
options.D: A graph showing the relationship between income and consumption

questions.explanation: A demand schedule is a table showing quantities demanded at different prices during a specified period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a demand curve?

options.A: A table showing quantities demanded at different prices
options.B: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded, other factors held constant
options.C: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity supplied
options.D: A graph showing the relationship between income and saving

questions.explanation: A demand curve is a graph showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded, other factors held constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an individual demand curve?

options.A: A curve showing the total quantity demanded by all consumers at each price
options.B: A curve showing the quantities one consumer is willing and able to buy at different prices
options.C: A curve showing the quantities producers are willing to sell at different prices
options.D: A curve showing the relationship between income and consumption

questions.explanation: An individual demand curve shows the quantities one consumer is willing and able to buy at different prices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is market demand?

options.A: The total quantity demanded by all consumers at each price, obtained by horizontally summing individual demand curves
options.B: The quantity demanded by a single consumer at a given price
options.C: The total quantity supplied by all producers at each price
options.D: The quantity demanded by the government

questions.explanation: Market demand is the total quantity demanded by all consumers at each price, obtained by horizontally summing individual demand curves.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What causes movement along a demand curve?

options.A: A change in the good's own price, with other demand determinants held constant
options.B: A change in consumer income
options.C: A change in tastes and preferences
options.D: A change in the price of related goods

questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price, with other demand determinants held constant, causes movement along a demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What causes a shift in the demand curve?

options.A: A change in the good's own price
options.B: Changes in income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, population or the number of buyers
options.C: A change in the quantity supplied
options.D: A change in the cost of production

questions.explanation: Changes in income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, population or the number of buyers cause a shift in the demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an increase in demand?

options.A: A rightward shift of the demand curve, meaning more is demanded at every given price
options.B: A leftward shift of the demand curve, meaning less is demanded at every given price
options.C: A movement along the demand curve due to a price change
options.D: A change in the quantity supplied

questions.explanation: An increase in demand is a rightward shift of the demand curve, meaning more is demanded at every given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a decrease in demand?

options.A: A rightward shift of the demand curve
options.B: A leftward shift of the demand curve, meaning less is demanded at every given price
options.C: A movement along the demand curve due to a price change
options.D: A change in the quantity supplied

questions.explanation: A decrease in demand is a leftward shift of the demand curve, meaning less is demanded at every given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a normal good?

options.A: A good for which demand generally decreases as consumer income increases
options.B: A good for which demand generally increases as consumer income increases, other things remaining equal
options.C: A good for which demand rises when its price rises
options.D: A good that has no substitutes

questions.explanation: A normal good is one for which demand generally increases as consumer income increases, other things remaining equal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an inferior good?

options.A: A good for which demand generally increases as consumer income increases
options.B: A good for which demand generally decreases as consumer income increases, other things remaining equal
options.C: A good for which demand rises when its price rises
options.D: A good that has many substitutes

questions.explanation: An inferior good is one for which demand generally decreases as consumer income increases, other things remaining equal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a Veblen good?

options.A: A good for which demand falls when its price rises
options.B: A good for which status or prestige effects can make higher prices increase its appeal to some consumers
options.C: A good that is consumed together with another good
options.D: A good that is available free of cost

questions.explanation: A Veblen good is a good for which status or prestige effects can make higher prices increase its appeal to some consumers.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is price elasticity of demand?

options.A: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price
options.B: The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price
options.C: The change in total revenue due to a price change
options.D: The change in quantity demanded due to a change in income

questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the formula for price elasticity of demand?

options.A: Ed = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price
options.B: Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price
options.C: Ed = percentage change in price ÷ percentage change in quantity demanded
options.D: Ed = change in quantity ÷ change in income

questions.explanation: Ed = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. It is usually negative under the ordinary law of demand; textbooks often discuss its absolute value.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: When is demand called elastic?

options.A: When the absolute value of price elasticity is greater than 1
options.B: When the absolute value of price elasticity is less than 1
options.C: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals 1
options.D: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals 0

questions.explanation: Demand is elastic when the absolute value of price elasticity is greater than 1.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: When is demand called inelastic?

options.A: When the absolute value of price elasticity is greater than 1
options.B: When the absolute value of price elasticity is less than 1
options.C: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals 1
options.D: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals infinity

questions.explanation: Demand is inelastic when the absolute value of price elasticity is less than 1.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: When is demand unitary elastic?

options.A: When the absolute value of price elasticity is greater than 1
options.B: When the absolute value of price elasticity is less than 1
options.C: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals 1
options.D: When the absolute value of price elasticity equals 0

questions.explanation: Demand is unitary elastic when the absolute value of price elasticity equals 1.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is income elasticity of demand?

options.A: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in consumer income
options.B: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price
options.C: The percentage change in demand for one good divided by the percentage change in the price of another good
options.D: The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price

questions.explanation: Income elasticity measures the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in consumer income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is cross elasticity of demand?

options.A: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income
options.B: The percentage change in demand for one good divided by the percentage change in the price of another good
options.C: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price
options.D: The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price

questions.explanation: Cross elasticity measures the percentage change in demand for one good divided by the percentage change in the price of another good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the sign of cross elasticity for substitute goods?

options.A: It is generally positive
options.B: It is generally negative
options.C: It is always zero
options.D: It is always equal to one

questions.explanation: For substitute goods, cross elasticity is generally positive.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the sign of cross elasticity for complementary goods?

options.A: It is generally positive
options.B: It is generally negative
options.C: It is always zero
options.D: It is always equal to one

questions.explanation: For complementary goods, cross elasticity is generally negative.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is supply?

options.A: The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices during a given period
options.B: The total quantity of a good available at a point in time
options.C: The quantity of a good that consumers are willing to buy
options.D: The price of a good in the market

questions.explanation: Supply is the quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different prices during a given period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the law of supply?

options.A: Other things remaining equal, quantity supplied generally falls when price rises
options.B: Other things remaining equal, quantity supplied generally rises when price rises and falls when price falls
options.C: Quantity supplied is always equal to quantity demanded
options.D: Quantity supplied is independent of price

questions.explanation: The law of supply states that, other things remaining equal, quantity supplied generally rises when price rises and falls when price falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: Why does the supply curve generally slope upward?

options.A: Higher prices can make additional production more profitable and justify using higher-cost resources
options.B: Because of diminishing marginal utility
options.C: Because of the income effect
options.D: Because of government regulation

questions.explanation: The supply curve generally slopes upward because higher prices can make additional production more profitable and justify using higher-cost resources.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a supply schedule?

options.A: A table showing quantities demanded at different prices
options.B: A table showing quantities supplied at different prices during a specified period
options.C: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity supplied
options.D: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded

questions.explanation: A supply schedule is a table showing quantities supplied at different prices during a specified period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a supply curve?

options.A: A table showing quantities supplied at different prices
options.B: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity supplied, other factors held constant
options.C: A graph showing the relationship between price and quantity demanded
options.D: A graph showing the relationship between income and consumption

questions.explanation: A supply curve is a graph showing the relationship between price and quantity supplied, other factors held constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What causes movement along a supply curve?

options.A: A change in input prices
options.B: A change in technology
options.C: A change in the good's own price, with other supply determinants held constant
options.D: A change in taxes

questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price, with other supply determinants held constant, causes movement along a supply curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What causes a shift in the supply curve?

options.A: A change in the good's own price
options.B: Changes in input prices, technology, taxes, subsidies, expectations, number of sellers, weather and production conditions
options.C: A change in consumer income
options.D: A change in consumer tastes

questions.explanation: Changes in input prices, technology, taxes, subsidies, expectations, number of sellers, weather and production conditions cause a shift in the supply curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is an increase in supply?

options.A: A rightward shift of the supply curve, meaning more is offered at every given price
options.B: A leftward shift of the supply curve, meaning less is offered at every given price
options.C: A movement along the supply curve due to a price change
options.D: A change in the quantity demanded

questions.explanation: An increase in supply is a rightward shift of the supply curve, meaning more is offered at every given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is a decrease in supply?

options.A: A rightward shift of the supply curve
options.B: A leftward shift of the supply curve, meaning less is offered at every given price
options.C: A movement along the supply curve due to a price change
options.D: A change in the quantity demanded

questions.explanation: A decrease in supply is a leftward shift of the supply curve, meaning less is offered at every given price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is price elasticity of supply?

options.A: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price
options.B: The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price
options.C: The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in income
options.D: The percentage change in price divided by the percentage change in quantity supplied

questions.explanation: Price elasticity of supply measures the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the formula for price elasticity of supply?

options.A: Es = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price
options.B: Es = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price
options.C: Es = percentage change in price ÷ percentage change in quantity supplied
options.D: Es = change in quantity supplied ÷ change in income

questions.explanation: Es = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is perfectly elastic supply?

options.A: A vertical supply curve
options.B: A horizontal supply curve at a particular price
options.C: A downward-sloping supply curve
options.D: An upward-sloping supply curve

questions.explanation: Perfectly elastic supply is represented by a horizontal supply curve at a particular price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is perfectly inelastic supply?

options.A: A horizontal supply curve
options.B: A vertical supply curve, where quantity supplied does not change with price
options.C: An upward-sloping supply curve
options.D: A downward-sloping supply curve

questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic supply is represented by a vertical supply curve, where quantity supplied does not change with price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: How does an increase in demand affect equilibrium price and quantity, assuming an upward-sloping supply curve?

options.A: It generally raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity
options.B: It generally lowers both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity
options.C: It raises equilibrium price but lowers equilibrium quantity
options.D: It has no effect on equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: An increase in demand generally raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity, assuming an upward-sloping supply curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: How does an increase in supply affect equilibrium price and quantity, assuming a downward-sloping demand curve?

options.A: It generally raises both equilibrium price and quantity
options.B: It generally lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity
options.C: It raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity
options.D: It has no effect on equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: An increase in supply generally lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity, assuming a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is the difference between stock and supply?

options.A: Stock is the quantity offered for sale at a price; supply is the total quantity available at a point in time
options.B: Stock is the total quantity available at a point in time; supply is the quantity offered for sale at a specified price during a period
options.C: Stock and supply are the same thing
options.D: Stock is the quantity demanded; supply is the quantity produced

questions.explanation: Stock is the total quantity available at a point in time; supply is the quantity offered for sale at a specified price during a period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.question: What is national income in the traditional textbook sense?

options.A: The total factor income earned by the normal residents of a country during an accounting period
options.B: The total value of goods and services produced within a country
options.C: The total value of exports
options.D: The total government revenue
